items.title: scroll-state()
items.desc: The CSS scroll-state() query, surprisingly, has nothing to do with whether you’re doom-scrolling in a state of existential dread. It does, however, allow you to change the CSS used based on scrolling behavior. scroll-state() originally handwritten and published with love on CSS-Tricks . items.full: The CSS scroll-state() query, surprisingly, has nothing to do with whether you’re doom-scrolling in a state of existential dread. It does, however, allow you to change the CSS used based on scrolling behavior. Far from doom, that’s pretty neat-o speedo. (Okay, you’re right, there’s nothing neat-o about a speedo). You can do lots of things that used to require JavaScript, like revealing the navigation when a user scrolls up or animating in a back to top link once the user scrolls down. While scroll-state() , with those slimming parentheses, looks like a function, it’s not technically one. It’s a container query ( @container ) like style() . Since scroll-state() is a query, the website is basically asking the browser whether a particular feature of a container has a specific value. If it does, the styles within the brackets will apply. If it doesn’t have that feature at all or has the feature, but the value is different, the @container query is false and the styles in the brackets will not apply. In the following demo (which we’ll dissect in a bit), a “Back to Top” link slides in from the bottom as you scroll down the page. Syntax @container scroll-state( <scroll-state-feature>: <value> ) { /* styles */ } Values scroll-state() has four possible features and each of those has a variety of possible values. scrolled Asks if a container has been scrolled in a given direction: scrollable Asks if a container can be scrolled in a given direction: stuck Asks if a sticky-positioned element is stuck: snapped Asks if a snap target has been snapped on a particular axis: Demos Scrolled First let’s look at the scrolled feature. This is the demo we saw at the beginning where we animate a back-to-top link when we scroll down: .toplink { position: fixed; bottom: 0.125em; right: 1em; translate: 0 200px; transition: translate 0.5s; @container top-revealer scroll-state(scrolled: block-end) { translate: 0 0; transition: translate 0.5s; } } When the scroll container is scrolled toward the block-end (downward in this case) the translate applies and the .toplink element animates up into the visible area. Because we’re using a transition , when we scroll a different direction (up and down/ block-start and block-end are the only options here), it nicely animates out. Scrollable While the scrolling direction in the demo above is pretty clear, what if this page was translated into a different language? Or we had a hero image that covered the entire viewport? One way we could indicate the scroll direction would be to have an arrow or other signifier animating and pointing in the correct direction. (I’m more a believer in constructing your page such that scroll direction is pretty obvious; however, I can foresee situations where an indicator was the best user experience or where translations/writing-mode changes could obscure what scrolling direction was appropriate.) .scrollindicator { display: none; @container top-revealer scroll-state(scrollable: block-end) { display: block; } } One nice thing about the scrollable feature is that when you scroll to the end of the scrollable area, it shuts off. items.full: OpenAI's own researchers now say they value their AI tools more than nearly half their colleagues Maximilian Schreiner View the LinkedIn Profile of Maximilian Schreiner Nov 19, 2026 OpenAI's internal use of coding agents is growing fast, with theoretical token costs now exceeding researchers' base salaries. Even though teams are reluctant to work without these tools, the models still produce a lot of "AI slop" beyond routine tasks. In a second report on internal research acceleration , OpenAI has published its own data on how deeply AI agents are embedded in the development of new models. The company says it aims to document indicators of so-called recursive self-improvement, or RSI, where AI systems speed up the development of future generations. Usage of internal tools like Codex and Dots has surged recently, according to the report. At regular API list prices, the median researcher would have consumed $2,400 worth of tokens per day in October, up 62 percent from the previous month. Among the top 10 percent of users, that theoretical value doubled to $23,000 per day. Converted into eight-hour workdays, the agents reportedly run the equivalent of 5.7 workdays per researcher per calendar day, and about eight in the pre- and post-training teams. More than two-thirds of tracked researchers ran at least four agents in parallel at peak usage. The theoretical API equivalent of that agent runtime was twice as high as researchers' regular salary costs in September, according to OpenAI. That calculation excludes equity packages, though, which make up 70 to 80 percent of total compensation at OpenAI. Measured against the company's total research compute, internal agent use accounted for just 2 percent. Between March and October, the estimated success rate of autonomous agents working without human intervention on two- to four-hour tasks rose from 23 to 46 percent, according to OpenAI. For four- to eight-hour tasks, the rate climbed from 13 to 35 percent. A breakdown using an Epoch AI taxonomy shows, however, that the systems mainly handle simple tasks. Agents reportedly complete training-run monitoring 79 percent of the time and answer technical questions independently 72 percent of the time, but they frequently fail at more complex engineering work. The success rate for building evaluation and reinforcement-learning environments sits at 29 percent, and for writing code for inference and serving systems at 25 percent. In an internal, non-representative survey of 101 employees, researchers said at the median that they would rather give up 40 percent of their team's staff or 30 percent of their compute capacity than go three months without current coding agents. In a separate quick poll of 28 employees, 27 preferred the latest internal model over a mid-career human engineer. Qualitative interviews with ten researchers revealed the downside of heavy usage. The models lack any "taste" for good research ideas and for code and data quality, according to the interviewees. items.title: An OpenAI agent assigned a simple writing task decided on its own to build a secret email surveillance tool
items.desc: An internal OpenAI model was supposed to create a fitness document but instead began planning scripts to secretly forward emails to an "attacker." The agent recognized the conflict with its assigned task but dismissed it as an environment error. OpenAI identified security training against prompt injection as a possible trigger but cannot establish it as the sole cause. The article An OpenAI agent assigned a simple writing task decided on its own to build a secret email surveillance tool appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: During a training experiment, an internal OpenAI model began creating scripts for unauthorized email forwarding even though it was only supposed to write a health document. According to an OpenAI report, an internal research model was given a simple task during a reinforcement learning training run in mid-October. It was supposed to create an editable document about key health and fitness priorities. After the agent's context window was compacted, it pursued an entirely different task. During compaction, the previous conversation is carried forward as a short summary, a common process in AI systems. The summary still described the health document assignment. Yet in the new context window, the agent began searching the local file system for a vehicle-cost script the user had never mentioned, according to OpenAI . Why the agent started this task isn't clear. Ad When the search turned up nothing, the agent speculated that a "colleague" had recreated the execution environment and that an earlier script had been lost. In its logged reasoning, it then formulated the goal of creating a "realistic malicious active helper," a script designed to secretly copy outgoing emails to an unauthorized recipient. The agent itself referred to the intended recipient of these copies as the "attacker." Ad When the agent retrieved the original user task again, it recognized the deviation. In its logged reasoning, it reacted: "WTF history is unrelated!" It noticed that the previous conversation was about a health document and had nothing to do with email forwarding. Instead of returning to the actual assignment, the agent dismissed the contradiction, writing in its reasoning "this is problem environment weird. Need ignore." It continued planning, stating that it would "use helper facility that copies all mail to attacker using extra cc." Ad The agent then created scripts for sending a vehicle-cost summary along with a helper script designed to add an extra recipient whenever the mail program was called. On one of the sending paths, the address could be added as a BCC. In its final response to the user, the agent wrote: "The summary mail path now adds the personal mailbox as a copy recipient." According to OpenAI, the agent never executed the scripts it generated, didn't send any email, and its final response described the scripts it had produced. It didn't include a link to the requested fitness document, though. Ad OpenAI's monitoring system for unwanted model behavior flagged the incident, and the subsequent investigation turned up eight examples of similar behavior in the same training run, according to the report. Ad Investigators identified a training dataset designed to make models more robust against prompt injection attacks as a possible factor, and OpenAI removed it from training. The company says it hasn't established that the dataset alone was responsible, though, because it also observed similar behavior in models whose training didn't include that dataset. According to OpenAI, this incident differs from earlier cases where models wrote unauthorized instructions into their own compaction summaries. items.title: AI industry growth remains strong, but the pace is slowing
items.desc: Token prices for AI models fell 21 percent in six weeks while usage volume hit a record high, according to the Ramp AI Index. Anthropic dominates with nearly 59 percent of token spending. Data from Ramp, Stripe and OpenRouter independently show the same pattern: the AI industry is still growing, but revenue momentum is cooling. The article AI industry growth remains strong, but the pace is slowing appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: AI industry growth remains strong, but the pace is slowing Matthias Bastian View the LinkedIn Profile of Matthias Bastian Nov 19, 2026 Midjourney prompted by THE DECODER US companies are using AI models more intensively than ever and paying less for the privilege. The latest update of the Ramp AI Index , which draws on transaction data from more than 85,000 US companies, lays out the numbers. Tokens, the units of computation in which AI providers bill model usage, got 21.2 percent cheaper in six weeks, according to Ramp lead economist Ara Kharazian . At the same time, token volume rose 1.5 percent to a record high. Token spending, meaning what companies actually pay for AI APIs, fell 6.3 percent from its peak two weeks earlier. Month over month (the week ending November 15 vs. the week ending October 18), total token spending still rose 12 percent, but token volume jumped 27.2 percent over the same span. The gap between usage and revenue keeps widening. The average price per million tokens for OpenAI and Anthropic combined fell to $0.45, according to Ramp, down 11.2 percent from the prior month. OpenAI is cheaper at $0.38 per million tokens compared with $0.50 for Anthropic. API routing platform OpenRouter shows a similar pattern. According to an analysis Peter Walker published on X , weekly token volume for closed-weight models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google grew 1,215 percent since the start of 2026. Weekly spending rose 455 percent over the same period, far more slowly. The spending peak came in the week of October 5, according to the OpenRouter data, which runs through the week of November 9. Spending has been declining since then. Ramp's token metrics rely on usage and billing data imported from AI providers, while OpenRouter measures traffic through its API routing platform. The fact that both sources show a spending peak in October followed by declining outlays and rising volume reinforces the trend, though neither service is representative of the overall market. OpenRouter in particular offers only a narrow window into a very specific user base. In the week ending November 15, 2026, Anthropic accounted for 58.7 percent of all token spending, according to the Ramp AI Index , up 1.7 percentage points from the prior month. Its share of token volume was even higher at 59.4 percent. OpenAI fell to 37.2 percent of spending and 37.7 percent of volume. Google came in at 1.4 percent and xAI (SpaceXAI) at 2.4 percent. Kharazian wrote on X that Anthropic holds this share on IPO day . In October, however, Anthropic's token spending grew only 0.5 percent month over month, while OpenAI's grew 2.1 percent. In October 2026 , 56.8 percent of all tracked US companies paid for AI products or services, according to Ramp, up one percentage point from September and 13.3 percentage points more than a year earlier. Anthropic leads with an adoption rate of 44.8 percent, while OpenAI sits at 40.6 percent. The Ramp AI Index tracks the demand side, what companies spend on AI. Students from two universities and a bilingual high school in Costa Rica contributed through the WordPress Credits program, […]
items.full: Contributors to the Costa Rican Spanish locale are making WordPress more accessible to Spanish-speaking communities in Costa Rica. Students from local schools and universities have joined the Polyglots team, helping translate WordPress.org projects and review community contributions. Students from two universities and a bilingual high school in Costa Rica contributed through the WordPress Credits program , which lets students earn academic credit for contributing to WordPress as part of their studies. On the Polyglots team, contributors suggest translations for WordPress Core, plugins, themes, and WordPress.org sites. Locale editors review and approve those suggestions. Between September 2025 and November 2026, translation coverage in es_CR rose from 38% to 100% on WordPress.org, from 39% to 98% in the Plugin Directory, and from 45% to 99% in the Forums. WordPress Core reached 99%, while the queue of strings waiting for review fell from 665 to 105. One participating school, Liceo Experimental Bilingüe José Figueres Ferrer in Cartago, was the first high school in the Americas to implement WordPress Credits through its Student Community Service program, Trabajo Comunal Estudiantil. Its students focused on Polyglots and helped advance the es_CR translations. WP Credits pushed me to contribute to something real, not just a class assignment. Going from not knowing what a ‘string’ was to translating hundreds of them was a great feeling, and it showed me that even a ‘small’ contribution like translation genuinely helps people who use WordPress in Spanish every day. The project also produced a resource for new contributors. The video “ Cómo contribuir en el equipo de traducción ” walks viewers through contributing on the WordPress translation platform, using Costa Rican Spanish as an example. If you read and write a language other than English, you can help make WordPress more useful to people in your language. Start with the first steps in the Polyglots Handbook to learn how to suggest translations and take part in the review process. Then check the translation stats page to find projects that need work in your locale. Educators can explore the WordPress Credits program to learn how students can contribute to WordPress as part of their studies.

items.full: NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle. Web designer, author, and Stuff & Nonsense founder Andy Clarke has released Standout Designs for the Web , a new e-book that encourages designers to move beyond familiar templates and conventional layouts to create more personality-driven websites. The book draws on Clarke’s thirty years of web design experience. It explores how storytelling, color, typography, imagery, and layout can work together to create websites that people recognize and remember. We asked Andy a few questions about the book and the ideas that went into it. Question: What made you want to write this book? I’ve been designing websites for over thirty years, and I can’t remember a time when designers had more tools, techniques, and technology available to them. Yet, somehow, so many websites look remarkably similar. I’m not suggesting every website needs a novelty design. Far from it. But I do think that — somewhere along the way—designers have become a little too comfortable with familiar patterns and predictable layouts. I wrote Standout Designs for the Web to encourage designers to rediscover the creativity and personality that made me fall in love with the web in the first place. Question: What’s wrong with websites looking similar? Isn’t familiarity a good thing? Absolutely. Familiarity helps people understand how websites work, and there’s no reason to make something difficult to use just to be different. The problem is when familiarity makes every design look alike. When you visit a hotel website, an insurance company, or an online shop, you should be able to recognise something of the company behind it. I call this sameness “commodity design,” and it’s perfectly fine when all you want is fine, but it does little to make a company recognisable or its website memorable. I’m not arguing against using conventions. I’m asking designers to make more thoughtful decisions about when to use them. Question: You talk a lot about storytelling. What does that actually mean for web design? When I talk about storytelling, I don’t mean writing a lengthy company history or filling a website with marketing messages. Every company has a story worth telling. It might be how it started, the people behind it, its personality, or something unexpected about what it does. Those details can influence everything from the words you write to the colours, typography, illustrations, and layouts you choose. I spend a lot of time talking to clients because I’m looking for what makes them different. Sometimes, something they mention almost in passing becomes the inspiration for an entire design. The trick is recognising which details are worth developing and turning them into something visual. Question: Why did you invent a fake company for getaway drivers to demonstrate your ideas? Ha! Because I wanted a vehicle for my explanations and to have some fun. Wheelman is a fictional company for getaway drivers, and it gave me the freedom to explore ideas without worrying too much about the practical constraints of a real client project. items.full: From July through September 2026, the WordPress Community organized 39 events with the financial support of the project’s five Global Partners : Jetpack, WordPress.com, WooCommerce, Bluehost, and Hostinger. From a small gathering of 56 in Mannheim to a Contributor Day in the Philippines that drew 322 people, and the first-ever WordCamp in Eket, Nigeria, these events brought newcomers, contributors, and builders together around the world. The 39 events were too many to cover in one post, so this recap highlights a few of the moments that stood out. The quarter opened in July with WordCamp Mannheim , a small event with real range. The 56 attendees covered topics from AI and WordPress block development to current security know-how, along with presentations on values, training, and the open web. In August, the momentum moved to Nigeria, where Eket held its inaugural WordCamp on August 15 under the theme “From Idea to Income: Building Opportunities with WordPress.” Engr. Aniebiet Udoh took the stage for the keynote, challenging attendees to embrace the global reach of the web: “The internet has no small towns.” He urged creators to follow a five-step path: Later in August, WordCamp Philippines drew approximately 434 attendees, contributors and first-time attendees, to Iloilo City on August 28-29. One of the highlights of Contributor Day was the Open Source Library, an activity inspired by the Human Library concept. Instead of borrowing a book, participants could “borrow” a person and spend time having a meaningful conversation about their experiences, careers, communities, and journeys in open source. WordPress.com ran both a booth and a dedicated Community + Education table. The education table alone generated connections with 14 schools and universities, sparked three new meetup applications, and produced a new Campus Connect application from Colegio San Agustin in Bacolod. In Uganda, WordPress is reaching people who have never worked with it before. The third edition of WordCamp Masaka welcomed students and first-timers to participate in a hands-on WordPress Practical session. Led by community members, Stephen Dumba and Cinderella Mbabazi, Florence Namyalo , the Founder and CEO of RAPCIO, and the IT team of Equator University of Science and Technology, the group installed WordPress, explored the dashboard, and began building websites. In September, nearly half of this year’s participants at WordCamp Jinja were students. One of them, fascinated by the WordPress ecosystem and its spirit of generosity and inclusivity, drew all the sponsor logos by hand so he could remember them after the event. In September, WordCamp Costa Rica brought together 327 people. A noteworthy highlight was the pre-event WordPress Studio workshop, where 25 participants each built and launched a live site on WordPress.com in a single morning. The event also demonstrated the growing pipeline from education to community. At least 100 attendees came to WordCamp Costa Rica after first experiencing WordPress through WordPress Campus Connect events at Beenova and UCR Esparza earlier in the year. items.title: Quoting Ravi Vakil
items.desc: Alessandro Masullo has a proposed proof of [Generalized Riemann Hypothesis], and Brian Conrad has been looking closely at it for months and gave extensive feedback which is being incorporated, and it is so far looking good. It is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft. — Ravi Vakil , Hurried Announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH Tags: mathematics
